mitochondria.definition: Tiny parts inside cells that turn food into energy the cell can use. They carry a small set of their own genes, separate from the cell's main DNA.

mitochondrial-derived-peptide.definition: A short peptide whose recipe sits in the mitochondria's own genes rather than in the cell's main DNA. MOTS-c and humanin are examples.

analogue.definition: A lab-made molecule built to look like a natural one, usually changed so that it lasts longer or acts more strongly.

aicar.definition: A small natural molecule inside cells that switches on AMPK, the cell's energy sensor. As a drug it is banned in sport.

telomere.definition: The protective caps at the ends of chromosomes. In most body cells they get a little shorter every time the cell divides.

telomerase.definition: An enzyme that rebuilds telomeres. Most body cells keep it switched off; many cancer cells switch it on, which helps them keep dividing.

pineal-gland.definition: A small gland deep in the brain that makes the hormone melatonin, mostly at night.

melatonin.definition: A hormone the pineal gland makes in the dark. It helps set the body's day-night rhythm.

epithalamin.definition: An extract made from the pineal glands of cattle and used in Russia. Epitalon was designed as a lab-made copy of one small part of it.

tetrapeptide.definition: A peptide made of exactly four amino acids joined in a chain. Epitalon is a tetrapeptide.

bdnf.definition: A growth factor in the brain that helps nerve cells survive and form new connections.

tuftsin.definition: A natural chain of four amino acids cut from an antibody. It stirs up immune cells that eat germs. Selank is built on it.

enkephalin.definition: A small natural opioid made by the body that damps down pain and stress signals. Enzymes in the blood break it down quickly.

nootropic.definition: A loose word for substances said to improve memory or thinking. It is not a medical diagnosis or a group of approved medicines.

benzodiazepine.definition: A group of anxiety and sleep medicines, such as diazepam. They work quickly but can cause drowsiness and dependence.

thymus.definition: A small organ behind the breastbone where T cells, a kind of white blood cell, learn their job. It shrinks with age.

dendritic-cell.definition: An immune cell that picks up pieces of germs and shows them to T cells, so the immune system knows what to attack.

toll-like-receptor.definition: A sensor on immune cells that recognises common features of germs and switches on an immune response.

immunomodulator.definition: A medicine that changes how the immune system works, turning parts of it up or down.

elisa.definition: A common lab test that uses antibodies to measure a substance in blood. It can give wrong results if the antibodies also stick to other molecules.

orphan-designation.definition: A label a regulator gives a medicine that is still being developed for a rare disease. It brings help for the developer. It is not an approval to sell the medicine.

senescence.definition: The state of a cell that has stopped dividing for good, for example because its telomeres have become too short. It is one of the body's brakes on cancer.

brown-fat.definition: A kind of body fat that burns energy to make heat, instead of storing it.

neurasthenia.definition: An older diagnosis for long-lasting tiredness and weakness, often with poor concentration and irritability.

trigeminal-neuralgia.definition: Sudden attacks of severe pain on one side of the face, coming from the nerve that carries feeling from the face.

national-marketing-authorisation.definition: A licence to sell a medicine given by one country's regulator. It applies in that country only, not in the rest of the EU.
